Guardian: NHS at risk of 'system failures' as demand for ADHD and autism care soars, inquiry finds. By Denis Campbell and Anna Bawden. On-page 'Fri 9 Oct 2026 00.01 BST', last modified 08.29 BST.
'The NHS in England is heading into a "world of system failures" as it struggles to cope with relentlessly rising demand for mental health, ADHD and autism care, leaving those affected desperate for support, a government-commissioned inquiry has found.'
Found an increasing risk of overdiagnosis of autism and ADHD and urged ministers to toughen regulation of the private clinics many people turn to because they cannot be assessed quickly by the NHS.
Called for access to care to be based primarily on a person's needs so fewer people face years-long waits for a formal diagnosis.
HARD FIGURE: the number of 16- to 64-year-olds with a common mental disorder increased from 15.5% in 1993 to 22.6% in 2024.
Mental distress has risen significantly across all age groups in England since the 1990s, especially the under-18s.
Companion pieces: 'No "snowflakes": mental health review says today's youth have it harder and harms are real' (https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/oct/09/fonagy-review-snowflakes-young-people-mental-health) and an explainer 'What has the Fonagy review found and what does it recommend?' (https://www.theguardian.com/society/2026/oct/09/key-findings-fonagy-nhs-mental-health-adhd-autism).
NOTE ON FRAMING: this headline leads on system failure and demand; the BBC leads on over-diagnosis risk; the GOV.UK release stresses that 'population-level prevalence of these conditions appears broadly stable'. Same review, three different emphases.
